Infectious Disease > General Infectious Disease Millions of Cancers Linked to Infections, Study Says — Four of the five leading infectious causes have "highly effective" prevention measures by Terrence Rudd, Staff Writer, MedPage Today October 1, 2026 • 3 min read Add MedPage Today on Google MedpageToday Key Takeaways Infections led to an estimated 2.3 million new cancer cases in 2024, including gastric cancer, cervical cancer, hepatocellular carcinoma, leukemias and lymphomas, and nasopharyngeal cancer. Helicobacter pylori, human papillomavirus, hepatitis B virus, Epstein-Barr virus, and hepatitis C virus accounted for nearly all cancers caused by infections. Four of the five leading infectious causes of cancer, as well as HIV, already have "highly effective" prevention measures, researchers said. Over 2 million new cancer cases were attributable to infections globally in 2024, according to an analysis of worldwide cancer incidence, highlighting the importance of effective prevention measures. Infections led to an estimated 2.3 million new cancer cases in 2024, including gastric cancer, cervical cancer, hepatocellular carcinoma, leukemias and lymphomas, and nasopharyngeal cancer, which accounted for 12% of all cancer cases worldwide. Among 12 carcinogenic infectious agents, the largest numbers of cancer cases were attributable to: Helicobacter pylori: 760,000 cases, population-attributable fraction (PAF) 4% Human papillomavirus (HPV): 750,000 cases, PAF 4% Hepatitis B virus (HBV): 360,000 cases, PAF 2% Epstein-Barr virus (EBV): 260,000 cases, PAF 1% Hepatitis C virus (HCV): 160,000 cases, PAF <1% Kaposi's sarcoma-associated herpesvirus (KSHV): 35,000 cases, PAF <1% Most cancers attributable to H. pylori were non-cardia gastric cancers (700,000 cases), while cervical cancer accounted for most HPV-attributable cases (600,000). HBV and HCV were responsible for 330,000 and 130,000 cases of hepatocellular carcinoma, respectively, while EBV led to 110,000 nasopharyngeal cancers, reported Harriet Rumgay, PhD, of the International Agency for Research on Cancer in Lyon, France, and colleagues in Lancet Oncologyopens in a new tab or window. "Our findings underscore the importance of accelerating control of infectious agents to achieve cancer prevention goals," Rumgay and colleagues wrote. Clinicians can help reach those goals through interventions such as HBV and HPV vaccination; testing and treatment for H. pylori, HBV, HCV, and HIV; and cervical screening programs, Rumgay told MedPage Today. Given those interventions, four of the five leading infectious causes of cancer, as well as HIV, already have "highly effective" prevention measures, she noted. Other measures can reduce transmission, such as safe injection practices, condom use, and HIV pre-exposure prophylaxis. The challenge lies in the infections that currently have no effective prevention tools, particularly EBV, Rumgay said. "A major priority is the development of vaccines against EBV, which causes several cancers and has also been linked to multiple sclerosis," she explained. New prevention tools are also needed for KSHV, particularly given that the KSHV-related cancer burden falls disproportionately on resource-limited countries in sub-Saharan Africa. Geography and infection prevalence present their own obstacles to taming infection-driven cancers, Rumgay added. For example, eastern Asia accounted for 42% of infection-attributable cancers in 2024, while sub-Saharan Africa was responsible for 25% of cases. In eastern Asia, H. pylori and HBV infections were behind a majority of cancer cases, while HPV was the biggest cause in sub-Saharan Africa. Measles Is, Too opens in a new tab or window Given regional variations in infection prevalence, healthcare infrastructure, vaccination coverage, and screening and treatment, "there is no single prevention strategy that will work equally well everywhere," Rumgay said. "As a result, prevention strategies need to be tailored to local infection and disease patterns and healthcare needs, while ensuring equitable access to effective interventions." Rumgay and colleagues analyzed 2024 national estimates of new cancer cases in people of any age from the Global Cancer Observatory's Cancer Today database and other registry data. They estimated the percentages of cases that could be attributed to 12 infectious agents classified as Group 1 carcinogens by the International Agency for Research on Cancer Monographs Program. For all cancers in 2024, the age-standardized incidence rate (ASIR) for cases caused by infectious agents was 22.7 cancer cases per 100,000 person-years. HPV had the highest ASIR, at 7.7 cases, followed by H. pylori (6.9), HBV (3.4), EBV (2.6), HCV (1.5), and KSHV (0.4). The share of new cancer cases driven by infectious agents varied by region. Sub-Saharan Africa had the highest PAF, at 25%, followed by northern Africa (16%), southeastern Asia (16%), eastern Asia (15%), and the Caribbean and Central America (13%). In contrast, northern Europe (4%), and Oceania, North America, and western Europe (all 5%), were well below the 12% global PAF. Study limitations included the lack of sex-specific PAFs, which may overlook sex-related differences in the percentages of infection-attributable cancer cases. Meet the five infections responsible for almost one in eight cancers worldwide

New estimates suggest infections were responsible for 2.3 million cancer cases worldwide in 2024.

  • 30 September 2026
  • by Linda Geddes

At a glance

A new analysis by the International Agency for Research on Cancer suggests that infections caused around 12% of all new cancers worldwide in 2024, amounting to roughly 2.3 million cases.

The vast majority of these cancers were caused by Helicobacter pylori, human papillomavirus (HPV), hepatitis B, Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) and hepatitis C.

More than three quarters of infection-related cancers occurred in low- and middle-income countries, where many people still lack access to effective prevention and treatment.

Infections caused around 12% of all new cancers worldwide in 2024, amounting to an estimated 2.3 million cases, according to an analysis by the International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC).

Despite progress in vaccination and screening, infection-related cancers remain a major global challenge, with the burden falling disproportionately on populations in low- and middle-income countries.

- Dr Harriet Rumgay, IARC's Cancer Surveillance Branch

Just five infections accounted for almost all of the estimated cases: Helicobacter pylori, human papillomavirus (HPV), hepatitis B, Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) and hepatitis C.

Many infection-related cancers are preventable through measures such as vaccination against HPV and hepatitis B, testing and treatment for H. pylori and viral hepatitis, or screening for HPV.

However, the report warned that access to these measures remains uneven. More than three quarters (77%) of infection-related cancers occurred in low- and middle-income countries, where financial, political and health-system barriers can limit access to prevention and treatment.

Eastern Asia had the greatest number of infection-related cancers, with an estimated 990,000 cases in 2024. This accounted for 42% of the global total and was largely driven by H. pylori and hepatitis B.

However, the burden was proportionally greatest in sub-Saharan Africa, where infections were responsible for around one in four new cancer cases, particularly HPV-related cancers.

“The findings underscore the major role that infection control can play in reducing the global cancer burden,” said study co-author Dr Harriet Rumgay of the IARC's Cancer Surveillance Branch. “Despite progress in vaccination and screening, infection-related cancers remain a major global challenge, with the burden falling disproportionately on populations in low- and middle-income countries.”

So, which infections are responsible for the greatest cancer burden and what can be done about them?

Helicobacter pylori

Topping the IARC’s list was H. pylori, a bacterium found in the lining of the stomach. It is usually acquired during childhood and can persist for decades if left untreated.

Although most people who are infected never develop cancer, it can cause persistent inflammation and other changes that increase the risk of stomach cancer.

According to the IARC analysis, the bacterium was responsible for an estimated 760,000 cancer cases worldwide in 2024, around 4% of all cancers diagnosed that year.

H. pylori can be treated with antibiotics, and studies suggest that doing so can reduce the incidence of stomach cancer by 36% and deaths from the disease by 22% in people who are infected with it.

However, so far, only a few countries have implemented population-level screen-and-treat programmes for the bacterium. Vaccines against H. pylori are also in development.

Human papillomavirus (HPV)

Close behind H. pylori, HPV was responsible for an estimated 750,000 cancer cases worldwide in 2024, around 4% of all new cancers.

HPV is extremely common, with around 80% of people thought to acquire at least one infection during their lifetime. Most infections clear by themselves, but persistent infection with certain high-risk types is responsible for almost all cases of cervical cancer, as well as a proportion of anal, penile, vaginal, vulval and throat cancers.

More than two decades of research has shown that HPV vaccines substantially reduce persistent HPV infections and precancerous cervical changes. Real-world studies are also now showing that HPV vaccination is reducing cervical cancer rates in countries that introduced it early on.

Hepatitis B

Hepatitis B was responsible for an estimated 360,000 cancer cases worldwide in 2024, around 2% of all new cancers. The virus infects the liver and, if infection becomes chronic, it can cause inflammation and damage that may eventually lead to cirrhosis or liver cancer.

Hepatitis B can be prevented through vaccination. Because the risk of developing chronic hepatitis B is particularly high when infection occurs early in life, the World Health Organization recommends that all babies receive a first dose of hepatitis B vaccine within 24 hours of birth, followed by two or three further doses.

A complete course provides 98–100% protection against infection, which can last for decades and probably for life.

Epstein-Barr virus (EBV)

EBV was linked to an estimated 260,000 cancer cases in 2024, making it the fourth largest infectious cause of cancer globally. EBV is extremely common, infecting around 95% of people worldwide and remaining in the body for life.

Most infections cause few or no symptoms, although the virus can cause glandular fever if it is first encountered during adolescence or adulthood.

EBV can also contribute to the development of cancers including Burkitt lymphoma, Hodgkin lymphoma and nasopharyngeal cancer. The virus is also increasingly being linked to stomach cancer.

Although there is currently no licensed vaccine against EBV, several candidates are currently in development.

Hepatitis C

Hepatitis C was responsible for an estimated 160,000 cancer cases worldwide in 2024. Like hepatitis B, the virus infects the liver and can cause a persistent infection that may eventually lead to cirrhosis or liver cancer.

There is currently no vaccine against hepatitis C, although researchers are trying to develop one. However, a short course of antiviral drugs can cure more than 95% of infections and substantially reduce people's risk of developing liver cancer.

The problem is that hepatitis C can remain symptomless for many years, so many remain unaware that they are infected. Globally, access to diagnosis and treatment is also limited.

Other infectious causes of cancer

The IARC analysis included seven further infections known to cause cancer in humans. These included Kaposi sarcoma-associated herpesvirus (KSHV), which causes Kaposi sarcoma; human T-cell lymphotropic virus type 1 (HTLV-1), which can cause a type of leukaemia; and Merkel cell polyomavirus, which is linked to a rare form of skin cancer.

The list also included three parasitic worms: Schistosoma haematobium, which is linked to bladder cancer, and the liver flukes Opisthorchis viverrini and Clonorchis sinensis, which can cause bile duct cancer. HIV was also included because, although it doesn’t directly cause cancer, the immune suppression it causes increases the risk of cancers associated with other infections.

While these infections accounted for a relatively small share of the global total, some are more important in certain regions. For example, KSHV contributed to the particularly high burden of infection-related cancers in sub-Saharan Africa, alongside HPV and HIV.

Most infections clear by themselves, but persistent infection with certain high-risk types is responsible for almost all cases of cervical cancer, as well as a proportion of anal, penile, vaginal, vulval and throat cancers. More than two decades of research has shown that HPV vaccines substantially reduce persistent HPV infections and precancerous cervical changes. Real-world studies are also now showing that HPV vaccination is reducing cervical cancer rates in countries that introduced it early on. Interested in more articles like this? Cancer breakthrough as personalised mRNA vaccine stops melanoma returning HPV vaccine means young women are no longer dying from cervical cancer in England Hepatitis B Hepatitis B was responsible for an estimated 360,000 cancer cases worldwide in 2024, around 2% of all new cancers. The virus infects the liver and, if infection becomes chronic, it can cause inflammation and damage that may eventually lead to cirrhosis or liver cancer. Hepatitis B can be prevented through vaccination. Because the risk of developing chronic hepatitis B is particularly high when infection occurs early in life, the World Health Organization recommends that all babies receive a first dose of hepatitis B vaccine within 24 hours of birth, followed by two or three further doses. A complete course provides 98–100% protection against infection, which can last for decades and probably for life. Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) EBV was linked to an estimated 260,000 cancer cases in 2024, making it the fourth largest infectious cause of cancer globally…

Written byAnastasia Scott Anastasia Scott Anastasia Scott is an Assistant Editor at Discover Magazine. Her work focuses on bringing clarity and creativity to scientific ideas. View Full Profile. Learn about our Editorial Policy. Sep 29, 2026, 9:30 PM | 3 min read Epstein-Barr Virus (Image Credit: Corona Borealis Studio/Shutterstock) Newsletter Sign up for our email newsletter for the latest science news Sign Up Epstein-Barr virus lives in nearly every adult on Earth, usually without causing any trouble. When it does lead to cancer, which cancer seems to depend on where you live. In Southeast Asia, it’s mostly tumors in the part of the throat behind the nose. In Europe and the Americas, it’s more often stomach cancer or lymphoma. That pattern shows up in a new global estimate of cancers caused by infections, published in The Lancet Oncology by researchers at the International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC). The study attributes 2.3 million new cancer cases in 2024, more than a tenth of the world’s total, to infections. Epstein-Barr, the virus behind mononucleosis (mono), was linked to about 260,000 of them, a total topped only by H. pylori, HPV, and hepatitis B. “This updated analysis shows that the landscape of infection-related cancers continues to evolve as scientific evidence advances,” said Gary Clifford, senior co-author of the study, in a press release. “It also highlights where future investments in new prevention tools could have the greatest impact, particularly for infections such as EBV, for which effective vaccines are not yet available.” Why One Virus Leads to Different Cancers Once someone catches Epstein-Barr, the virus stays in their body for life, hidden inside some of their cells. Proteins the virus makes can push those cells to keep dividing, one step on the path to cancer. You have 1 more free article (1 of 2) Have an account? log in Subscribe today for full access and support our journalism. Explore All Options Yet only a small share of the carriers ever develop a related cancer. That gap, along with the way the cancers vary from region to region, hints that other factors are involved. Among the possibilities are people's genes, their diets and surroundings, other infections, and weakened immunity. The split is the strongest in Southeast Asia, where about 80 percent of the region’s 34,000 Epstein-Barr cancers were nasopharyngeal (the tumors that form in the upper throat behind the nose). Nasopharyngeal cancer also led in Sub-Saharan Africa. There, though, Burkitt lymphoma, a fast-growing cancer that often affects children, made up a notable share, and the authors flag malaria, widespread in the region, as a possible contributor. Stomach cancer only recently joined the list of cancers counted for Epstein-Barr in these global estimates, along with two more types of lymphoma. Those newly counted cancers make up about 100,000 of the virus’s 260,000 cases. Read More: Viagra May Limit Cancer’s Spread by Trapping Cholesterol Inside Cells The Cancers We Already Know How to Prevent Just five of the 12 infections, including Epstein-Barr, caused nearly all of the 2.3 million cases. H. pylori, a common stomach bacterium, was linked to about 760,000 cases, almost all of them stomach cancers and more than half in eastern Asia. It can be cleared with antibiotics, and stomach cancer rates have fallen in many places as sanitation has improved and fewer infections are passed between family members. HPV, linked to about 750,000 cases, is treated in the study as the cause of every cervical cancer, about 600,000 in 2024. It also causes throat, anal, and penile cancers. A single vaccine dose protects as well as two or three, which could help reach more girls in sub-Saharan Africa, where the rate of HPV-caused cancer is more than twice the global average. Hepatitis B can be prevented with a vaccine too, and antiviral drugs treat hepatitis B and C. But these tools reach some places much better than others, and low- and middle-income countries accounted for 77 percent of the cases. No Vaccines for Epstein-Barr Epstein-Barr has no vaccine or reliable way to control it once someone is infected, although several vaccines are being tested. Most people reading this probably picked up Epstein-Barr long ago, maybe from a parent’s kiss, or a shared spoon, and will never give it a second thought. A vaccine could one day let some of those who would otherwise get cancer from it do the same. This article is not offering medical advice and should be used for informational purposes only. Daily roundup Spark: Our top stories Just 5 Infections Responsible For More Than 2 Million New Cancer Cases Annually Health29 September 2026 By Jess Cockerill (Kateryna Kon/Science Photo Library RF/Getty Images) Cancer may seem like an inevitable part of life, but there are so many factors that can help reduce your risk. When we think about reducing cancer risk, we usually think of lifestyle factors: smoking, alcohol consumption, exercise. But a new study by a team of cancer epidemiologists, published in The Lancet Oncology, highlights just how much infections actually contribute to your cancer risk. Based on global data, infections were linked to 12 percent of all cancers that were diagnosed in 2024. That's 2.3 million new cancer cases. Five key pathogens were responsible for nearly all of those infection-linked cases. The most common offender was a stomach bacterium, Helicobacter pylori, which was involved in 4 percent of the total cancers diagnosed in 2024 – that's 760,000 cases. H. pylori is a really common bug: statistically speaking, every second person in the world is infected with it. For most people, infection with H. pylori causes no symptoms, but certain strains can cause gastric ulcers and ultimately stomach cancers. The human papillomavirus (HPV) was also linked to 4 percent of the total new cancers diagnosed in 2024, which is 750,000 cases. frameborder="0′′ allow="accelerometer; autoplay; clipboard-write; encrypted-media; gyroscope; picture-in-picture; web-share" referrerpolicy="strict-origin-when-cross-origin" allowfullscreen> Hepatitis B virus (HBV) was linked to 2 percent of new cases, Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) was linked to 1 percent, and hepatitis C virus (HCV) was linked to less than 1 percent. EBV is a newcomer to this list. Since previous global estimates were published, the evidence that EBV causes cancer has grown substantially. It's pretty freaky to think that these infections, which can already make us very sick in their own right, could also lead to cancer, but these findings also give us an opportunity. They suggest proper treatment and prevention of these infections could make a really big difference to cancer rates across the world. "Our updated estimates highlight the continued importance of infection control in global cancer prevention strategies," lead author Harriet Rumgay and her colleagues note. "Many carcinogenic infectious agents have existing or potential preventive interventions, including vaccines, diagnostics, treatments, and safe injection practices." For many of these pathogens, it's a matter of actually getting those public health interventions to people. "Despite progress in vaccination and screening, infection-related cancers remain a major challenge globally, with persistent inequities especially impacting low-income and middle-income countries," the authors add. Three-quarters of infection-related cancers came from low-income and middle-income countries, predominantly in eastern Asia, African nations south of the Sahara, and southeastern Asia. The bulk of infection-linked cancer diagnoses in 2024 were made in eastern Asia, making up 42 percent of the global total. The infections linked to those diagnoses were mainly H. pylori and HBV. Getting more people vaccinated for HPV (especially men, who have often not been targeted for HPV vaccines) and HBV should make a huge dent in global cancer rates, but for H. pylori, the answer is not so simple. "So far, there has been little progress in developing H. pylori vaccines or highly effective H. pylori therapies that can minimize ineffective antibiotic exposure, which would be highly impactful for controlling gastric cancer globally," the authors write. We also have no vaccine or any other methods to control the spread of EBV (which infects about 95 percent of adults), though several clinical trials for vaccines are underway. "Although investment in the development of new preventive vaccinations for EBV, H. pylori, and Kaposi's sarcoma [another cancer linked to viruses] is key, many prevention strategies are known to be cost-effective," the authors write. "Unfortunately, such strategies are often underused due to societal, financial, and political barriers, often in the settings that need them most. "Considering the overwhelming economic and social costs of cancer, investment in prevention is crucial." The research was published in The Lancet Oncology. NewsPricingLoginSign up free News·Discovery Discovery nChroma Bio's epigenetic silencer therapy shows sustained HBV suppression in preclinical models Edited by Robert McTiernan·September 28, 2026·2 min read Researchers at Boston-based genetic medicines company nChroma Bio published preclinical data in Nature Biomedical Engineering supporting CRMA-1001, an LNP-delivered epigenetic silencer now in Phase I/II development for chronic hepatitis B (CHB). The study showed durable suppression of viral markers from both integrated and episomal HBV DNA without cutting the underlying DNA sequence. Why it matters: Current nucleoside/nucleotide analogue therapies suppress HBV replication but do not eliminate or durably silence the cccDNA and integrated HBV DNA reservoirs that sustain chronic infection. CRMA-1001 is designed to switch off transcription from both reservoirs through targeted DNA methylation, potentially enabling durable viral suppression from a finite treatment course. CRMA-1001 delivers mRNA encoding the EE7000 epigenetic silencer together with an HBV-targeting guide RNA in liver-directed lipid nanoparticles. The complex uses catalytically inactive Cas9 to localize transcriptional repressors and DNA methyltransferase activity to HBV DNA, depositing methylation marks without introducing DNA breaks. In mouse models, a single dose produced dose-dependent suppression of HBV antigens that persisted for up to 207 days. In an episomal HBV model, three monthly doses left approximately 90% of animals with undetectable HBsAg and HBV DNA at six months. The therapy also suppressed HBsAg and HBeAg in HBV-infected primary human hepatocytes, with methylation of cccDNA confirmed. A non-human primate toxicology program supported clinical entry, although transient liver transaminase elevations were observed at the highest tested dose. The preclinical package supported progression into a Phase I/II trial (NCT07200193), which dosed its first patient in January 2026. The study is evaluating single and multiple ascending doses in up to 66 adults with CHB who remain on background nucleoside/nucleotide analogue therapy. The AllSci BriefFree, systematic R&D and deal news. Daily. Subscribe CRMA-1001 enters an emerging field of therapies aimed directly at persistent HBV DNA reservoirs. Tune Therapeutics has already reported early clinical proof-of-concept with TUNE-401, another epigenetic silencer targeting HBV cccDNA, while Precision BioSciences is testing PBGENE-HBV, which takes a different approach by using the ARCUS nuclease platform to cut and eliminate viral DNA rather than silence it. The study was funded by nChroma Bio and included collaborators from the San Raffaele Telethon Institute for Gene Therapy and the Istituto Nazionale Genetica Molecolare in Milan. virus,EBV)约26万例,可致鼻咽癌、部分胃癌及霍奇金淋巴瘤(Hodgkin lymphoma);丙型肝炎病毒(HCV)约16万例。上述五种几乎占感染相关癌症的绝大部分。低收入和中等收入国家约占感染相关病例的77%。东亚病例最多,约99万例,占全球该类病例的42%;撒哈拉以南非洲占比最高,当地约四分之一新发癌症与感染有关。 IARC新闻稿称,此次把名单扩至12种病原体,并纳入新确认的关联,例如HIV与部分癌症、梅克尔细胞多瘤病毒(Merkel cell polyomavirus)与侵袭性皮肤癌,以及EBV与胃癌等。共同作者、癌症流行病学家加里·克利福德(Gary Clifford)对CBC表示,已知感染源也被发现可导致更多癌种。 据CBC采访,麦克马斯特大学(McMaster University)胃肠病学家保罗·莫阿耶迪(Paul Moayyedi)称,加拿大每年约有2000人死于胃癌,过程十分痛苦。幽门螺杆菌多在童年经拥挤居住、卫生条件较差的环境感染;多数感染者可长期健康生活,部分人会发展为溃疡或胃癌。筛查可用血液、呼气、粪便或胃镜,治疗通常为约两周联合抗生素。他希望对高风险人群——如有胃癌家族史者、部分原住民社区——开展筛查。另据2019年相关研究,加拿大因感染引起的癌症约占4%;曾在麦吉尔大学(McGill University)带领加国团队的卡雷纳·沃莱斯基(Karena Volesky)估计,仍相当于每年7000多例诊断。北美数字低于全球,但幽门螺杆菌与HPV仍是最常见感染源。加国儿童HPV疫苗接种使宫颈癌发病率下降,卫生机构目标包括在2040年前消除宫颈癌。 原新闻链接 雨露肝霖 雨露肝霖 发表于上海 慢乙肝生物标志物 消化新前沿 企业/ 关注 互相关注 2026年9月11日- 13日,“中部肝病与感染学术会议(CCIFLDI 2026)暨人畜共患传染病重症诊治全国重点实验室2026年学术会议”在湖北省武汉市隆重召开。 深度解析医学证据,DeepEvidence为你支撑决策 编者按 2026年9月11日- 13日,“中部肝病与感染学术会议(CCIFLDI 2026)暨人畜共患传染病重症诊治全国重点实验室2026年学术会议”在湖北省武汉市隆重召开。 9月12日下午,华中科技大学同济医学院附属同济医院吴迪教授进行了有关“Biomarker-Guided Therapy toward Functional Cure of Chronic Hepatitis B”的专题报告。肝霖君与您分享精彩内容。 慢乙肝难以实现临床治愈,其最大障碍不仅在于cccDNA和整合HBV DNA会持续表达HBsAg,更关键的是,在持续存在的病毒与抗原负荷下,宿主免疫系统处于一种“失能”状态。因此,亟需通过免疫调控来重塑宿主的免疫应答,从而最终抑制HBV复制,实现临床治愈。 2014年,基于OSST研究以及相应的循证医学证据,该团队提出了“免疫失能”是实现临床治愈的最大障碍,现阶段可用的核苷(酸)类似物(NA)和聚乙二醇干扰素α(PegIFNα)联合治疗可促进优势患者实现临床治愈。 基于前期开展的一系列临床试验,以及国内外的循证医学依据,由宁琴教授牵头,联合全球26位知名专家共同制定的《慢性乙型肝炎功能性治愈导航:专家共识2.0》于2025年正式发布,总结了慢乙肝临床治愈的路线图。 OSST研究:首次通过RCT研究证实,对于NAs经治、获得完全病毒学应答的慢乙肝患者,采用有限疗程的PegIFNα治疗可实现临床治愈。在停药后1年内,超过85%的患者维持HBsAg清除,实现真正的“临床治愈”。 OSST研究不仅证实了PegIFNα的治疗有效性,研究团队还据此建立了优势患者的识别方法,并提出了基线指导治疗(BGT)和应答指导治疗(RGT)策略。 Anchor研究:纳入HBsAg < 3000 IU/mL的慢乙肝患者。采用多靶点联合策略,同样以PegIFNα为核心治疗方案,延长PegIFNα疗程,并联合使用GM-CSF等免疫调节剂。 结果表明,PegIFNα + NAs组96周的HBsAg清除率超30%,HBsAb阳性率超35%。停药24周后,HBsAg清除率为27.7%,HBsAb阳性率为25.0%。 HBsAg是最关键的HBsAg清除预测指标,根据基线HBsAg水平进行分层,HBsAg < 100 IU/mL的患者HBsAg清除率为66%,100 < HBsAg < 1000 IU/mL的患者为40%。 除了HBsAg基线水平,其早期的变化幅度以及HBV RNA的早期下降幅度也可预测临床治愈率。 年龄也是一个重要的预测因素,年龄越小,越容易获得临床治愈。 结合患者治疗结束时的指标进行分析,发现治疗结束时HBcrAg < 4 log10 U/mL及HBsAb > 2 log10 mIU/mL的患者更容易维持稳定的免疫应答状态,并且更容易实现停药后持久的HBsAg清除。 系列研究证实,基于免疫调节的联合治疗策略可有效重塑宿主的免疫“失能”状态。基于此,该团队归纳总结出BGT、RGT及停药后持续应答的预测模型,并将其整合至乙肝治疗路径图中,为慢乙肝临床治疗决策提供了循证依据。 此外,HBV整合也可用于预测临床治愈。基于Anchor研究发现基线HBV整合水平越低的患者,越容易实现临床治愈。 相关免疫学指标也在持续探索中。研究发现,免疫重建不全可能是介导PegIFNα序贯治疗后病毒学复发的关键机制。此类患者的特征是单核细胞表面TLR2低水平表达,以及CD8+ T细胞表面PD-1高水平表达。 靶向上述双靶点,通过协同调节先天免疫与适应性免疫,能否进一步改善患者的治疗应答? 对此,该团队设计了一项概念验证性、小样本、探索性、RCT研究——Oceancure 05研究。纳入NA经治、HBV DNA < 20 IU/mL、250 IU/mL < HBsAg < 5000 IU/mL的慢乙肝患者,分为NAs单药治疗组、NAs + TLR7激动剂组及NAs + TLR7激动剂 + PD-L1单抗组。 结果发现,三联治疗可诱导更大幅度的HBsAg下降,平均降幅为0.45 log10 IU/mL,显著高于NAs单药组和二联治疗组。且停药后,患者的HBsAg下降幅度相对稳定,未出现大幅反弹。安全性方面,未出现严重不良反应和死亡。常见的不良反应包括甲状腺炎及ALT升高。 在该研究中发现了与PegIFNα治疗类似的现象,即早期ALT升高以及早期HBsAg的快速下降与治疗应答密切相关。 本研究检测了不同外周血单核细胞(PBMCs)表面PD-L1的表达。结果显示,NAs联合TLR7激动剂可上调各亚群PD-L1的表达,而三联治疗则能有效抑制这一上调过程。且HBsAg下降幅度越大的患者,其PD-L1下调更为显著。 研究评估了不同治疗方案下HBV特异性细胞毒性T淋巴细胞(CTL)的应答情况。结果显示,三联治疗可显著恢复HBV特异性CTL的功能。进一步分析表明,三联治疗在CTL应答的广度与强度上均显著优于二联及NAs单药治疗。此外,通过对非初始CD8+ T细胞的差异基因表达分析发现,效应相关基因呈现高表达,且PD-1阻断相关基因亦存在显著差异表达。 研究发现,在不同细胞亚群中,MDSC表面的PD-L1水平与HBV特异性CTL应答呈显著负相关,且与病毒学指标密切相关,提示该细胞亚群中的PD-1可能在三联治疗中起到核心作用。体外功能验证实验表明,在去除MDSC的培养体系中,三联治疗能显著增强PBMC的IFN分泌,并提升CTL的细胞毒性及杀伤功能。 综上,本研究证实,协同靶向天然免疫与适应性免疫可进一步促进HBsAg应答。鉴于入组患者基线HBsAg水平较高,未来需进一步优化治疗方案。 ASO(反义寡核苷酸)是靶向HBV RNA的单链核酸聚合物,可减少病毒蛋白的表达、降低HBV DNA水平,并可能通过激活TLR8通路,激活先天免疫应答。 Bepirovirsen的B-Clear研究分析发现应答人群集中在基线HBsAg低水平的患者。B-Well研究结果显示,在整个队列中,19%的患者实现临床治愈。在HBsAg < 1000 IU/mL的患者中,临床治愈率为26%。基线HBsAg水平越低,临床治愈率越高。 在其临床研究的事后分析中也发现了部分患者出现ALT 升高伴随HBsAg快速下降,提示其可能存在一定的免疫调节作用。 总结 病毒抑制联合免疫调节是目前实现临床治愈的关键策略。 整合基线、治疗早期及治疗结束后的标志物,有助于精准制定旨在实现临床治愈的联合治疗策略。 新型生物标志物,尤其是免疫学标志物,值得进一步探索,以指导新型联合治疗策略。 阅读全文 微信扫一扫 分享 版权声明:
